content:
hi! i'm fairly new to lean (my background is in a different field) but i've played a solitaire variant called Elevens a lot and wondered what the actual odds of winning were. i couldn't find any exact numbers anywhere, so i figured i'd try to see if i could use LLMs to help compute them. (the bigger goal is Klondike, but i know that's a whole different beast.)

the main things i ended up proving were a confluence theorem (any two legal moves from the same position lead to equally winnable states, so the outcome is entirely determined by the initial shuffle. obvious if you've played this variant before, but i wanted to try to formalize it) and exact win probabilities (≈10.689% for the standard game and ≈19.923% for a variant where you can flip a card from the pile when you get stuck).

the entry point is ElevensChallenge.lean, which imports Basic.lean (definitions for the game, only imports Mathlib) and the repo has a comparator config :

https://github.com/shinyswellow/elevens-lean

happy to get feedback on whether the formalization is being done sensibly, or if there's anything worth fixing
Did you use AI to generate the code?

(oh sorry, I guess the clue is in the channel!). I guess the thing I then wanted to flag is that probably you didn't read your code, and the AI will not learn from feedback given about the code, so I would imagine that most people will be extremely unmotivated to give you any feedback. The community here is all well aware that for a sufficiently simple project it's now possible to get AI to do it, so my feedback is "it doesn't surprise me at all that you can do this".

I posted some interesting questions about the process of AI writing lean - #Autoformalization > questions of interest in autoformalization (as separate from the formal output itself). If you write up something more of interest along those lines that could also get more replies.

thanks! i'll take a look at the thread. like i mentioned, i'm new to Lean and haven't really learned much about it yet, but the question was of personal interest to me, which was my primary motivation for pursuing the answer, since i couldn't find an exact win probability online (wikipedia simply says "a little over 1 in 10" and it wasn't an included variant any of the many solitaire papers i read exploring this.)

i definitely don't think it's of any particular interest to anyone from the Lean formalization aspect and in fact it seems like from what i have been learning about Lean it might have been overkill. but i've been able to understand the language a bit better by reviewing the LLM's output for my problem and spending a bit more time reading discussions in this community, so who knows? maybe i'll return and can find something interesting to contribute Lean-wise. for now i'm pivoting towards looking at reinforcement learning techniques to improve klondike draw 3 machine play bounds.

the paper for the elevens result is in the github in case anyone in the future stumbles on this and wants to know what the exact win probabilities of those variations of solitaire are.

You can combine the paper and the formalization using verso - e.g. a half-baked project of mine https://rkirov.github.io/sudoku_theory/SudokuTheory/Defs/Puzzle/ but can give you an idea of what I mean.
